newsitem.title: USA: Twenty-nine states okayed for infrastructure banks.
newsitem.headline: Twenty-nine states okayed for infrastructure banks.

text.p: The Clinton Administration said Thursday it gave 29 more states the green light to set up transportation infrastructure banks and that it is awarding a total $150 million to the 39 banks nationwide.

State infrastructure banks are pools of money that can be used to finance projects like roads, bridges, and mass transit systems. States can leverage the dollars through issuance of tax-exempt bonds, although few use that option currently.

Ten states already take part in U.S. Department of Transportation's infrastructure bank pilot program. As of June 1, 1997, those states had designated $80 million of federal dollars and raised over $42 million in matching funds to capitalize the banks, the department said in a statement.
Congress recently expanded the pilot, and twenty-nine states applied and were approved, the department said.
Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater said each of the 39 states will get a share of $150 million for the programs.
He said that by the end of fiscal 1998, the first 10 pilots will have designated $324 million of regular federal transportation grants to support up to $1.6 billion in projects.
Clinton is seeking $900 million for state infrastructure banks in the administration's proposal to reauthorize the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act.
